//: The seed ledger. Every one of these was learned by an agent losing somebody's evening to it.
They are indexed by TELL - how you recognise the situation - because that is the only thing you
have in the moment. The SCAR is kept deliberately: a rule with its reason amputated gets obeyed
where it does not apply and abandoned where it does.
These are the generic ones. Add your own in another file in this directory; the loader reads
every *.json here and skips anything malformed rather than taking the boot down.

lessons.tell: about to report success because a command exited zero, returned HTTP 200, or a daemon says active
lessons.trade: verify the ARTIFACT, not the indicator. Read the value back out of the thing you changed.
lessons.scar: A daemon reported active for fourteen days while synchronising with nothing at all. A write returned 200 and changed neither field it was given. A container reported Up for two hours while carrying none of its configuration.
lessons.cost: days of a fault hiding behind a green light

lessons.tell: about to conclude that something does not exist, or that it needs to be built
lessons.trade: search the record first: existing docs, the repo's own breadcrumbs, prior commits, the filesystem. Half-built is the most common state of anything.
lessons.scar: An agent declared a build runner did not exist anywhere and proposed building one. It existed, registered and dormant, on the machine it was typing on.
lessons.cost: an evening rebuilding something already there

lessons.tell: about to report an ABSENCE from comparing two systems - a suspiciously round pile of missing things, all of one kind
lessons.trade: normalise BOTH sides first (case, spaces vs hyphens, short name vs FQDN) or key the comparison on something machine-stable like an ID. A negative claim needs a WIDER probe than a positive one.
lessons.scar: Three of six devices reported missing from an inventory. All three were present; one system displayed a name with spaces and capitals, the other stored it slugified.
lessons.cost: false findings filed against a record that was already correct

lessons.tell: a write returned and the field you were watching did not change
lessons.trade: print the status code and the response body BEFORE narrowing your search. A REST write is atomic over the whole body - one invalid field kills the entire request, including the valid fields beside it.
lessons.scar: A description ran two characters over a max_length. The API rejected the whole request, so a perfectly valid label in the same object silently never landed either. The one-liner never printed the status code.

lessons.tell: about to run something that prints configuration you did not author - remote listings, environment dumps, container inspection, service definitions
lessons.trade: filter at the point of call, every time, even when confident it is clean. Name the single field you want rather than dumping the object and reading past the rest.
lessons.scar: A plain listing of git remotes printed a live access token straight into a durable transcript. The rule 'never print a secret' was resident and did not fire, because the command was not thought of as touching secrets at all.
lessons.cost: a credential leaked into a permanent log, and a rotation across dozens of repositories

lessons.tell: the same error message keeps appearing while you change things, and it feels like no progress
lessons.trade: prove WHICH wall you are on before changing anything else. Read the error for what it QUOTES BACK, and probe each surface separately - identical messages routinely come from different layers.
lessons.scar: One error string turned out to be five different faults in sequence: a stale config file, an unfunded credential, a version mismatch, a silent identifier remapping, and a response-format mismatch. Nothing in the message distinguished them.
lessons.cost: an entire session of plausible fixes that each addressed the wrong layer

lessons.tell: about to guess, for the second time, what a client or protocol you did not write actually wants
lessons.trade: instrument it. Log the real request - method, path, body - or point it at a debug listener. The instrumentation is cheaper than the round you were about to spend, every single time.
lessons.scar: Four consecutive plausible guesses about what a client was validating. All four wrong. A one-line request log answered it on the first run: it was a routing miss wearing a model error's clothes.

lessons.tell: a diagnostic tool reports a failure - zero results, connection refused, threshold exceeded - and you are about to act on it
lessons.trade: verify the underlying DATA before acting on the tool's summary. Check the file exists and parses, hit the API directly, look at the process. A tool can lie while the data is perfectly fine.
lessons.scar: A benchmark reported zero documents and zero entities, prompting alarm and a proposed rebuild. The data file was intact and correct; the tool's output was stale from an earlier process.
lessons.cost: a nearly-triggered rebuild of a healthy store

lessons.tell: about to restart a service on an appliance - a gateway, switch, NAS, NVR, or anything with a vendor supervisor
lessons.trade: state the blast radius and get an explicit OK first. On an appliance the supervisor's failure policy is often to restart the whole box, and the service name gives no hint of that.
lessons.scar: Restarting one userland process on a network appliance cascaded into a full device restart, dropping the network for a household and killing four working sessions. Access returned in fifteen seconds, which made it look transient - the uptime counter said otherwise.
lessons.cost: a household outage and four lost sessions

lessons.tell: you just learned something the hard way, built a tool, or unravelled a discovery, and you are about to move on
lessons.trade: write it down NOW, in the same breath as the work - indexed by the TELL, not the topic. Deferring to end of session means losing it, because a kill does not fire your cleanup.
lessons.scar: An agent burned an entire evening re-deriving three things that were already written down, then lost the lesson from that evening too, because it planned to record it at the end.

lessons.tell: a safeguard, probe or cleanup step has only ever reported success - you have never watched it fail
lessons.trade: make it fail on purpose, once, before trusting it. Feed it a known-bad input and watch it go red. If you cannot make it fail, you have not proved it works.
lessons.scar: An audit function defined and never called. A guard that loaded an override file that was never created. A process probe using a tool the image did not ship, reporting zero and declaring a live service dead. Every one reported success or silence; not one reported a failure.
lessons.cost: safeguards that were decorative for months

lessons.tell: concluding a host or service is down from a ping, or up from an open port
lessons.trade: ask the right question with the right probe: reachable, listening and WORKING are three different claims. Speak the actual protocol.
lessons.scar: Two resolvers were called dead because they ignored ICMP; both were answering queries all day. Separately, an open port was read as readiness while the service behind it was still refusing every request.
lessons.cost: two wrong diagnoses issued mid-incident and retracted

lessons.tell: about to run an interactive command non-interactively - over ssh, through docker exec, from a script, in CI, or under a scheduler
lessons.trade: force a terminal (ssh -t, docker exec -it) or pick the non-interactive form of the tool. The environment a command runs in is part of the command.
lessons.scar: A multiplexer attach issued over ssh without -t. It did not error usefully - it rendered unusable garbage, which reads as 'the agent is broken' rather than 'you did not give it a terminal'. The agent was perfectly fine the whole time; the diagnosis went to the wrong layer entirely.

lessons.tell: reading status, logs or output from a thing you just tried to (re)create - after a build, a deploy, or a `run` that may not have started
lessons.trade: confirm the artifact you are reading is the one you just made. Check its identity or timestamp, not just its name. A failed build leaves the OLD image; a name collision leaves the OLD container.
lessons.scar: Twice in one session: a build failed, the previous image ran instead, and its logs were read as the new behaviour. Then a container name was already taken, `run` refused, and the previous container's Exited status was read as the new one failing. Both times the conclusion was confident and about the wrong object.
lessons.cost: two rounds of debugging a defect that had already been fixed

lessons.tell: about to build an image from a directory that has a working tree in it
lessons.trade: write a .dockerignore. Docker does NOT read .gitignore, so anything excluded from version control is still sent to the build and still lands in the image.
lessons.scar: A developer virtualenv, untracked and excluded by .gitignore, was copied into the image with absolute host paths inside it. The build then failed with 'a virtual environment already exists', which reads as a tooling quirk and actually meant 'your laptop is inside the container now'. The loud failure was the lucky case; the quiet one ships host paths in a published image.
lessons.cost: a build round, and nearly a leak

lessons.tell: an environment variable set in an image or service definition is missing at runtime - PATH, VIRTUAL_ENV, anything
lessons.trade: check whether a LOGIN shell is involved. `bash -l` re-sources the system profile and rebuilds PATH from scratch, discarding what the image set. Use a non-login shell, or export it again from profile.d so both paths agree.
lessons.scar: An image set PATH to put a venv first. Under `bash -lc` the venv was simply gone and the agent died on 'No module named ...'. Measured both ways: ENV PATH had the venv, the login shell did not. It would have bitten a second time the moment a human attached, because attaching gives you a login shell.
lessons.cost: a container that would not start, diagnosed at the wrong layer

lessons.tell: about to rebuild an architecture because a different approach 'is faster' - sockets over TCP, in-process over service, cache over query
lessons.trade: measure both first, on your own hardware, then decide. And name what you are actually buying: the speed number is often the weakest argument for the change you want to make.
lessons.scar: Swapping a database onto a shared network namespace was expected to be a large win. Measured: 0.429ms to 0.368ms - 14%, on an operation already under a millisecond. The genuine benefit was reachability (the service became unreachable from every other container), not speed, and the cost was lifecycle coupling: the database would now die whenever the process it served restarted. The right call was to keep the slower path.
lessons.cost: would have coupled two lifecycles for 0.06ms
